evidence.claim: NM 536 winds up the eastern side of the Sandia Mountains to a dead end at Sandia Crest.
evidence.quote: NM 536's western terminus is a dead end at Sandia Crest and the eastern terminus is in San Antonito, at NM 14.

evidence.claim: The climb reaches a ridge forested mainly with spruce and fir.
evidence.quote: The Crest is heavily forested, mostly with spruce and fir.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service calls the route the Sandia Crest National Scenic Byway and highlights its panoramic views of Central New Mexico and sheltered picnic grounds.
evidence.quote: drive the Sandia Crest National Scenic Byway to take in spectacular panoramic views of Central New Mexico and to enjoy many other recreational opportunities. The Sandia Crest Scenic Byway 536, has several newly remodeled picnic grounds with shelters

evidence.claim: The Forest Service completed a dirt road to the crest in 1927.
evidence.quote: In 1927, the US Forest Service completed a dirt road to Sandia Crest.

evidence.claim: Paving followed in 1960 to improve access to La Madera Ski Area.
evidence.quote: The roadway was paved in 1960 to improve access to La Madera Ski Area

evidence.claim: The new road replaced a journey through potholes and mud; sections of the old dirt road remain visible south of it.
evidence.quote: Sections of the old dirt road are still visible to the south of the new road.

evidence.claim: La Madera became Sandia Peak Ski Area in 1962.
evidence.quote: In 1962 Nordhaus changed the name of the resort to Sandia Peak Ski Area

evidence.claim: Start at NM 14 in San Antonito and follow NM 536 toward the ski area’s base on the east slope.
evidence.quote: the eastern terminus is in San Antonito, at NM 14.

evidence.claim: Continue to Sandia Crest, where a viewing area and communications towers occupy the road’s end.
evidence.quote: Located on the Crest at the western terminus of Sandia Crest Rd (NM 536) is a scenic viewing area

evidence.claim: The west side drops toward Albuquerque and the Rio Grande Valley, while the eastern slope descends toward the plains.
evidence.quote: To the east, the range slopes down from the Crest and merges into the plains below. On the west side of the Crest is a cliff; the range dramatically drops over 4,000 feet (1,000 metres) in elevation over 2 miles (3 kilometres) of horizontal distance to the Rio Grande Valley and city of Albuquerque below.

evidence.claim: NM 536 winds up the eastern side of the Sandia Mountains to a dead end at Sandia Crest.

evidence.claim: The new road replaced a journey through potholes and mud; sections of the old dirt road remain visible south of it.

evidence.quote: The resort is accessed from the east side of the mountains via Sandia Crest Rd (NM 536), which provides access to the base of the ski area

evidence.claim: Continue to Sandia Crest, where a viewing area and communications towers occupy the road’s end.

evidence.claim: La Madera began with a rope tow, not a chairlift.
evidence.quote: The club then opened La Madera Ski Area in 1936 with a 1,500 foot (460 m) rope tow.

evidence.claim: The Albuquerque Ski Club cleared runs at Tree Springs in 1935 and opened the ski area the following year.
evidence.quote: cleared ski runs in the Sandia Mountains at Tree Springs in 1935. The club then opened La Madera Ski Area in 1936

evidence.claim: Its 1,500-foot tow offered two rides for 50 cents.
evidence.quote: with a 1,500 foot (460 m) rope tow. Two trips on the rope tow cost 50 cents.

evidence.claim: A second tow followed in 1937, along with a lodge built with Civilian Conservation Corps help.
evidence.quote: The following year, a second rope tow was installed to Panoramic Point, and a ski lodge, built with the help of members of the CCC  , was constructed.

evidence.claim: The resort closed to the public during World War II.
evidence.quote: The resort closed to the public at the outbreak of World War II and remained so until the war concluded.

evidence.claim: Afterward, a T-bar lift replaced the upper rope tow in 1946.
evidence.quote: After the war, the upper rope tow was removed and a state-of-the-art T-bar lift, Constam Lift, was installed in 1946.

evidence.claim: Kiwanis Cabin is a stone ruin on the crest between Sandia Crest House and the ski resort.
evidence.quote: The Kiwanis Cabin, the ruins of the cabin of the Kiwanis Group of the Civilian Conservation Corps, is located on the Crest between the Sandia Crest House and the ski resort

evidence.claim: Its pueblo-style architecture overlooks the Rio Grande Valley.
evidence.quote: a stone cabin on the crest in pueblo-style architecture, overlooking the Rio Grande Valley.

evidence.claim: Hikers visit the ruins; the cabin is an excursion along the ridge.
evidence.quote: The ruins of the cabin are today a popular site with hikers.

evidence.claim: Kiwanis Cabin is a stone ruin on the crest between Sandia Crest House and the ski resort.

evidence.claim: Sandia Crest is a long ridge rather than a pointed summit.
evidence.quote: Instead of a true summit or topographic peak, this range climbs to a long ridge line.

evidence.claim: Its western side drops more than 4,000 feet in two horizontal miles toward the Rio Grande Valley and Albuquerque.
evidence.quote: the range dramatically drops over 4,000 feet (1,000 metres) in elevation over 2 miles (3 kilometres) of horizontal distance to the Rio Grande Valley and city of Albuquerque below.

evidence.claim: Spruce and fir cover much of the crest, where radio and television antennas also stand.
evidence.quote: The Crest is heavily forested, mostly with spruce and fir. There are communication radio antennae of various radio and television stations situated at the top.

evidence.claim: The road ends at a viewing area by Sandia Crest House.
evidence.quote: Located on the Crest at the western terminus of Sandia Crest Rd (NM 536) is a scenic viewing area, the Sandia Crest House

evidence.claim: The tramway reaches a different point on the crestline, about 1.5 miles south of Sandia Crest, above the ski area.
evidence.quote: The Sandia Peak Tramway ascends from the west side to a point on the crestline about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) south of Sandia Crest, at the top of the Sandia Peak Ski Area

evidence.claim: Another proposal, Skyline Drive, would have extended a road along the crest. By autumn 1969, five miles of forest had been cleared, but a campaign of postcards and petitions halted construction.
evidence.quote: by autumn of 1969, 5 miles (8 kilometres) of forest along the crest was cleared for the new road. Alarmed locals started a campaign which included postcards and petitions, and successfully halted construction.

evidence.claim: Another proposal, Skyline Drive, would have extended a road along the crest.
evidence.quote: Included with the plan was Skyline Drive, a scenic highway that would have run for about 8 miles (13 kilometres) from La Madera Ski Area in the south, along the crest line

evidence.claim: Road access comes from the east via NM 536; the tramway approaches from the Albuquerque side and delivers riders to the ski summit.
evidence.quote: The resort is accessed from the east side of the mountains via Sandia Crest Rd (NM 536), which provides access to the base of the ski area, and from the west side via the tramway

evidence.claim: The crest also marks the western boundary of an 1819 land grant established by Governor Facundo Melgares, which included San Miguel de Carnuel and San Antonio Pueblo.
evidence.quote: In 1819, then Governor of Santa Fe de Nuevo México Facundo Melgares established a land grant in the mountains, including the town of San Miguel de Carnuel and the San Antonio Pueblo. The land grant used Sandia Crest as its western boundary.
